Looks like it's the same thing as Ritalin, which I took as a kid. I was too young to remember anything about it, but my mom took me off of it with a quickness.

I was the poster child for Hyper Activity in the 70s, now affectionately referred to as ADHD. Growing up, this was definitely a curse. I had poor grades, got in trouble - A LOT, couldn't do home work, chores were, well, a chore. Then I found two things: Weed, and computers. Weed replaced the Ritalin, which had it's own set of curses, and computers gave me an outlet.

The ever changing world of computers, along with myriad of tasks that a computer could perform, gave me that minute to minute, hour to hour, day to day, change of scenery that allowed me to prosper.

Today, I see it as a gift. I can work for hours if necessary, and can multi-task better than anyone around me.

The key is finding something that can hold your interest, but that has tons of variety. Woodworking can be that way, computers obviously, but there are certainly others. The only other advice is to stay off the prescriptions. I tried a plethora of different drugs over the years with Ritalin being the least of all evils. Weed was really a life saver for me. It provided the calming affect without the debilitating drug affects. I could concentrate, I could focus, and I could control the impulses without feeling like a zombie.

Not saying that weed is the solution for everyone, but it was for me... well, that and technology.

Good luck!

I have read up on this idea of "hyper focusing" that people with ADHD can perform when tasks are interesting and engaging. I found that out myself when I discovered photography with a brand new DSLR camera in which I knew nothing about. I began reading the manual and mastered the technical aspects of my camera without distractions in a couple of days.

For me the gift has been that my memory is pretty good, to the point it will scare people how well I can remember things. Someone can read off a credit card number to me and I can recall it for the next 15 minutes. That was incredibly helpful when working in a tech support call center. The other side to that sword edge is that my memory is polarizing when it comes to recall. I either remember things well to nearly eidetic, or I can barely recall them if at all.

In school, I was awful when it came to grades because of homework. I was out of school so it was off my mind. But when I was in class, I was pretty good. It wasn't until my late 20's that I was diagnosed and medicated. The medication has been a relief for me, I no longer struggle at work, I can keep a consistent energy level, and I no longer need to drink an inhuman amount of caffeine to remain focused.

When I opened up about it to my family (what kind of grown man has ADHD?!) everyone was really understanding. In fact most of them said, individually and verbatim, "Oh, that explains a lot of things..."

I always thought of it in a positive light. People with adhd are impatiant until they lock onto something that really interests them they tend to have incredible focus. They also tend to be out of the box thinkers. I think it has advantages and disadvantages.

You'll be fine. Don't worry. It shouldn't matter where in her cycle she is, because you only need Plan B if she IS in the fertile period. If she's not currently fertile, you wouldn't need Plan B at all. Of course the difficulty of predicting fertility is one of the reasons we need pharmaceutical birth control, but Plan B should be effective no matter where she is in her cycle. I also would not worry at all if her cycle is irregular. High doses of hormones will confuse your body for a while, and that's totally normal.

If she's concerned about her weight, I would recommend talking to a pharmacist. Often they can help with these sorts of technical questions without having to escalate to a doctor's appointment.
